# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why4: As described, the screen shows a question and hint with only a Continue action, so there are no options, rows, chips or value box to judge.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed and the hint reassures me that answers are unaffected, but "pilot" drifts a little from my real offer, which is ordering a pair with free returns.
screens.instead: Do you want people who finish to be able to ask to try the glasses? (Yes, let them ask / Not now) Optional, and it doesn't change their answers.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers get asked belongs just before the study goes out, but the hint says people on this account will read and tap, so the question looks already settled.
screens.why2: "Who should ask" is plain, but "runs on its own AI" and "needs Keel's credits" need a second read, and I can't tell whether I have a choice or what "the face" means.
screens.why3: I know my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can easily judge whether they should read and tap or face an interviewer.
screens.why4: The only choice visible is a face Keel has preselected, which is odd beside a hint that says people will read and tap, and nothing says whether a talking interviewer would be captioned for people who can't hear it.
screens.why5: The screen rewrites nothing I typed and does not change what my study means; it only asks how the questions reach people.
screens.instead: How should people answer your questions? Options: They read and tap (included) / An AI interviewer asks them, with captions on screen (uses Keel's credits).

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it is obvious why I am asked how people will answer, and for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents it really matters.
screens.why2: Text only is instantly clear, but "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud" took me a second read to see it means how many spoken answers get understood, and "needs Keel's credits" does not say what it costs.
screens.why3: I know my people are deaf and hard of hearing, many prefer reading to listening, and some do not speak, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and my true answer is there, but the AI option is odd for my audience because it sells spoken questions and audio accuracy without saying whether the questions are captioned, and "Hear it" is the only preview it offers.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed here, and the choice of Text only is shown as mine without altering the study's meaning.
screens.instead: How should they answer? Text only: they read each question and tap or type. AI interviewer: a face on video asks each question aloud with captions on screen, and they talk, type or tap (uses Keel's credits). Let them choose: they pick when they open the link (uses Keel's credits).

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, the last thing before sending is who receives the link, so the question is obviously in its place.
screens.why2: "Who gets a link?" and the three descriptions read plainly on first pass, and I only pause briefly at "Contacts page" before the explanation makes it clear.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already know, finding new ones, or posting in a community where they gather, so I can answer this from my own outreach.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and an open group link are distinct and cover how I would reach people, and my true answer of people I know by name is there.
screens.why5: The screen makes no claim about my idea and my pick of people I know by name is kept, so nothing I typed has changed meaning.

screens.why1: As the very first question it is obvious why they ask, because it checks whether I am someone who deals with hearing people at all before going further.
screens.why2: Hearing people is the phrase I and other deaf people use every day, and I understand the question on first reading.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people in a normal week, because it is my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, they do not overlap, and a gate question needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of talking with hearing people every week and tells me nothing about a product or company.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two short options, so I could take it in once and answer, though saying I'll read 2 options before a plain yes or no is slightly stiff.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask if I lost the thread with them this past week, because that sets up the story that follows.
screens.why2: Lose track of a conversation is exactly what happens to me and I understand it on first reading, though I might wonder if it means one missed bit or the whole thread.
screens.why3: I know whether this happened to me in the last seven days because it happens often and I remember when it does.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and the first chip fits, but there are two escapes where there should be one, and I can't recall one particular conversation is wordy and sits oddly on a yes-or-no about whether it happened at all.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's situation of a conversation with hearing people being hard to follow, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: The spoken form is short, one question, ending in yes or no, which is easy to catch once if I can hear the interviewer at all, and the chips are not said so nothing extra has to be held.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes; No; or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: I just said I lost track of a conversation with hearing people, and the kicker says part 2 is an idea to consider, so it is obvious why this card comes now.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses, an app and eye contact are all everyday words for me, and I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: Fast or noisy conversations and trying to keep eye contact while following along are exactly my week, so I can picture this in my own life.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is a deliberate Imagine card that says plainly what the thing is and marks the benefit as what its builders believe, and nothing feels like inside talk, though 'the wearer' is a bit of a product word.
screens.why6: It says well in short sentences, but 'inside the lens' comes late in a long clause and 'read the words while keeping eye contact' repeats 'You read the words' just before it, so it is slightly less easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps. When a conversation with hearing people is too fast or too noisy to follow, you wear lightweight glasses with an app. Live captions of what people nearby are saying appear in the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Straight after the idea, it makes sense to ask whether I had my phone on me, because that decides whether something like this could have worked in that conversation.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but 'with you and online' is two things in one, and 'your last conversation' doesn't say it means one with hearing people.
screens.why3: I nearly always know if my phone was on me and had signal, because I rely on it to communicate with hearing people.
screens.why4: Yes, No and the 'I can't tell' chip fit, but 'Mostly' and 'Partly' overlap and don't tell me which to pick if I had my phone but no signal.
screens.why5: AirCaps appears only as the idea I was deliberately shown, and the question is a practical one with no sales talk or insider terms.
screens.why6: It is short and the options are easy to hold, but 'with you and online' packs two checks into one breath, and 'Mostly; Partly' is hard to tell apart when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Did you have your phone with you, and was it online? Yes, with me and online; With me, but not online; or Not with me. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about my last conversation, it makes sense to ask whether AirCaps would have helped in it.
screens.why2: "Made it go better" is clear enough, but "it" needs a second thought because the conversation was named on the screen before, and the bare name AirCaps tells me nothing unless I remember the card.
screens.why3: I know how that conversation went and where I got lost, but I have never used AirCaps, so how much better it would have gone is partly a guess.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover what I could say without overlapping, and I can't tell fits because I may not know without trying it.
screens.why5: It names the idea only because the card is shown on purpose, and no business talk or founder terms reach me.
screens.why6: It is short with four options I can hold, but when heard alone "it" has nothing to point to and "AirCaps" is an unfamiliar name that could be misheard.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people: would AirCaps have made it go better for you, or not? A lot better; A little better; No difference; Worse; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: After being asked if AirCaps would have helped and whether my phone was with me, it makes sense to ask whether I'd bother with the setup step.
screens.why2: Pairing glasses to a phone is the same thing I already do with hearing aids or Bluetooth, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know how I feel about pairing devices from my hearing aids, but I have never used these glasses, so my answer is partly a guess at how it would go.
screens.why4: The options mostly cover it and I can't tell fits, but Probably not and No sit close together and there is no Probably yes to balance them, while Only if it connected without any trouble is a condition almost anyone would pick.
screens.why5: AirCaps is named on purpose in the idea card, and the pairing step reads as a plain fact about it with no company talk reaching me.
screens.why6: It is short with one question and the list is easy to hold, but Only if it connected without any trouble is a mouthful beside three very short options.
screens.instead: AirCaps means pairing the glasses to your phone. Would you do that, or not? Yes; Yes, if it pairs the first time; Probably not; or No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: It follows straight on from my answer about pairing the glasses, so I can see exactly why you are asking me this now.
screens.why2: The words are everyday ones, but "look like" is a bit vague for something as practical as connecting glasses to a phone, so I might need a second read to know you mean what should happen when I set them up.
screens.why3: I know what it is like to fuss with phones and hearing devices that drop out mid-conversation, so I can say what no trouble would mean for me.
screens.why4: There are no options on this screen, only a box to type in.
screens.why5: It stays with the pairing question and my own answer, and nothing new about the product or the people behind it reaches me.
screens.why6: It is two short sentences with one clear question and nothing awkward to say, so I could take it in once and answer.
screens.instead: You said only if it connected without any trouble. What would have to happen when you set up the glasses for that to be true?
